query: For single-phase ZrB2 ceramic, which requires preparation temperatures above 2300 °C and may lack the strength and structural integrity needed for service, what single intervention could lower the required preparation temperature and reduce the holes and eventual component failure caused by prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention and its mechanism, predict its performance compared with conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2, define the relevant preparation and service boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and describe a controlled preparation, integrity, and long-duration exposure experiment that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Switching from a conventional powder-sintering route to a liquid‐phase precursor synthesis for ZrB2 will lower the required sintering temperature and produce a denser, ultrafine-grained microstructure that is less prone to pore formation during prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventionally prepared single-phase ZrB2 produced by high-temperature (>2300 °C) powder sintering, which typically exhibits coarser grain size and residual porosity that makes it vulnerable to liquid-induced degradation.
generation.intervention: Adopt a liquid-phase precursor method (e.g., using molecularly mixed zirconium and boron precursors) to synthesize ZrB2 powders that can be densified at a lower temperature (~1800 °C).
generation.conditions: Synthesis performed at lower temperature (around 1800 °C) under controlled atmosphere to achieve full reaction and densification, and service conditions involving prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath at typical operating temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of ultrafine, uniformly distributed ZrB2 grains with fewer residual pores, and possibly a transient low-melting phase at sintering boundaries that aids in pore elimination.
generation.mechanism: The liquid precursor method enables molecular-level mixing of the zirconium and boron sources, thereby dramatically reducing the diffusion distances needed for reaction. This promotes densification at a lower temperature, resulting in a refined microstructure with minimized porosity. In service, the denser and more uniform microstructure will resist the infiltration and corrosive attack from a liquid plating bath, reducing the formation of holes and associated material failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally prepared ZrB2, the liquid precursor-synthesized ceramic will achieve similar or better mechanical strength with significantly reduced porosity and enhanced resistance to liquid-induced degradation during extended exposure.
generation.baseline: Conventionally sintered single-phase ZrB2 prepared above 2300 °C that typically shows higher porosity, larger grain sizes, and a greater tendency to develop holes and fail upon prolonged exposure to a liquid plating bath.
generation.boundary: This intervention is applicable for single-phase ZrB2 ceramics where the processing temperature can be reduced to around 1800 °C with the liquid precursor method, and the service environment is defined by the liquid plating bath conditions (temperature, chemistry, and duration) relevant to typical applications.
generation.uncertainty: While promising evidence from similar high-entropy ceramic systems (e.g., PMC10707663) supports the effectiveness of liquid precursor methods in reducing sintering temperatures, the exact quantitative gains in densification, mechanical strength, and long-term resistance to liquid exposure for pure ZrB2 remain to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of single-phase ZrB2 samples: one group using the conventional high-temperature (>2300 °C) powder-sintering process, and the other using the proposed liquid-phase precursor method with sintering at ~1800 °C. Ensure both groups are processed under otherwise identical atmospheric and pressure conditions. After sintering, characterize each group for density, microstructure (grain size and porosity via SEM/TEM), and mechanical properties.
measurements: After a standardized long-duration exposure to a simulated liquid plating bath, re-assess the samples for the presence and extent of hole formation using high-resolution imaging and perform mechanical integrity tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the liquid precursor-synthesized samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in density (i.e., reduced porosity), mechanical strength, and resistance to hole formation after liquid plating bath exposure compared to the conventionally prepared samples.

## Abstract
AbstractA nano-dual-phase powder with ultra-fine grain size was synthesized by the liquid precursor method at 1200 °C. A series of single-phase high-entropy ceramic powders ((Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Mo)B2, (Ti, Zr, Hf, Nb, Ta, Mo)B2) with high purity (C content less than 0.9 wt% and O content less than 0.7 wt%) and ultrafine (average grain sizes of 340–570 nm) were successfully synthesized at 1800 °C. The sample of (TiZrHfNbTa)B2 exhibited a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) structure, and the metal elements were uniformly distributed at the nanoscale, microscale, and macroscale. This method did not apply to the preparation of all high-entropy ceramic powders and was unfavorable for the formation of single-phase high-entropy borides when the size difference factor exceeded 3.9%. The present work provides a guide for the development of ceramic-based composites through precursor impregnation pyrolysis.Keywords: liquid-phase precursor method, high-entropy diboride powders, solid solutions, microstructure, pyrolysis mechanism
